p: The word heads Nahum 1:1, Habakkuk 1:1, Zechariah 9:1 and 12:1, and this book.
b: The Hebrew massa' comes from the verb nasa', 'lift', and older English Bibles translate it 'burden', a weight the prophet carries. It heads a few prophetic books and oracles (Nahum 1:1; Habakkuk 1:1; Isaiah 13:1). In the Twelve, the last three units open this way: the two oracles of Zechariah 9-14 (Zechariah 9:1; Zechariah 12:1) and Malachi. Some redaction critics use this to argue that Zechariah 9-14 and Malachi were once a three-part collection, with Malachi's heading added to give the Twelve three closing oracles. That is a view, not a settled result. The Plain uses 'oracle', as in the other books of the Twelve.

t: Malachi: a name or a title?
p: The word means 'my messenger' (3:1). The book gives no father, town or date, unlike Haggai or Zechariah.
b: Malakhi is Hebrew for 'my messenger', the same word as in 3:1. Two views divide scholars. Some take it as a personal name, a short form of a name such as Malachiah. Others think an editor took the word from 3:1 and made it the prophet's name, since the book is otherwise anonymous, like Zechariah 9-14. The Greek (Swete's text) reads 'by the hand of his messenger', which treats it as a title. Jewish and Christian tradition went further. The Targum Jonathan says his name was Ezra the scribe, and Jerome also discusses the identification with Ezra. The Talmud (Megillah 15a) records three views: that he was Mordecai, that he was Ezra, and that Malachi was his real name. None of these can be checked.

p: The first word of the LORD in the book is a statement of love, answered with doubt.
b: The verb is Hebrew 'ahav in a form that states a lasting fact: 'I have loved you, and I still do.' In the language of ancient treaties, 'love' was the loyalty owed between a great king and his people, and Deuteronomy uses it that way of the LORD's choice of Israel (Deuteronomy 7:7-8). Malachi opens with this claim and the people's answer is a question, which is why the book is written as a dispute. The word is not only a feeling. What the prophet will point to is an act: Edom's ruin and Israel's survival.

a: But you say, "How have you loved us?"
p: Eight times the people answer the LORD with a question. Scholars call the form a disputation.
b: Eight times the people answer the LORD with a question (1:2, 6, 7; 2:14, 17; 3:7, 8, 13), each introduced by 'and you say'. The Plain uses the same English each time: 'But you say'. The pattern is charge, objection, reply. Adrian Graffy's book on the disputation speech in the prophets (1984) reserves that name for the prophets' habit of quoting the people's words in order to refute them. Micah 2:6-11 and Haggai 1:2-4 quote the people in the same way; Malachi does it throughout. Some commentators think it reflects a teaching style in which the prophet answers objections a doubting audience actually raised; others treat it as a literary device, with the objections the prophet's own. Either way the book lets the people speak, and so shows what they were thinking.

p: Esau is the father of Edom, so the question is about two neighbor nations that were also family.
b: In Genesis, Esau and Jacob are twin brothers, and Esau is the ancestor of Edom (Genesis 25:25-30; Genesis 36:1). Israel's law said an Edomite is a brother (Deuteronomy 23:7), but the prophets also remembered Edom's part in the fall of Jerusalem in about 586 BC (Obadiah 1:10-12; Psalm 137:7; Lamentations 4:21-22; Ezekiel 35). Malachi's point is that the two brothers' fates now differ: Jacob's descendants are back in the land and Edom's country is a waste. The archaeology of Edom in this period does not give a simple picture of ruin (see the note on 1:3), and Malachi does not name the cause.
r: Genesis 25:23-26; Genesis 36:1; Deuteronomy 23:7; Obadiah 1:10-12; Psalm 137:7; Lamentations 4:21-22; Ezekiel 35:1-15

t: 'I hated': a word of choice and rejection
p: In Hebrew, 'hate' can mean 'not choose', as with Leah. Paul quotes the line in Romans 9:13.
b: Hebrew sane', 'hate', is often the opposite of 'choose' or 'love' in family and covenant speech. Leah is 'hated' when Jacob loves Rachel more (Genesis 29:30-33), and a man's 'hated' wife in Deuteronomy 21:15-17 is the less favored one. Jesus uses the same idiom for the cost of following him (Luke 14:26, compared with Matthew 10:37). So many scholars hold that Malachi says 'I chose Jacob and not Esau', not that the LORD feels personal hatred. Malachi speaks of nations, Edom's mountains and Israel's land, not of anyone's eternal destiny. Paul quotes the line to argue about God's free choice: "I loved Jacob, but I hated Esau." (Romans 9:13). The churches read Paul's use differently (see the card).

a: I made his mountains a waste
p: Edom's high country is wrecked and left to jackals, as Isaiah, Jeremiah and Obadiah had promised.
b: Edom's heartland is the high plateau of Seir, east of the Arabah (Genesis 36:8). Isaiah 34 pictures it as a place of ruin where jackals live (Isaiah 34:13), and Jeremiah and Obadiah say its strongholds will fall (Jeremiah 49:17-18; Obadiah 1:8-9). Malachi says it has happened. Excavation does not simply show a ruin: Piotr Bienkowski reports that the major Edomite sites of Busayra (Buseirah), Tall al-Khalayfi and Tawilan stayed occupied into the Persian period, while other Edomite sites were abandoned by the end of the 6th century BC. How Malachi's 'waste' fits that evidence is left open.

p: Edom will be known by the LORD's verdict. The 'territory' answers Israel's 'border' in 1:5.
b: The Hebrew is gevul rish'ah, 'territory of wickedness'. The word 'territory' (gevul) comes back in 1:5, where the LORD is great 'beyond Israel's border': Edom's border is named by its sin, and Israel's is passed by God's greatness. The Greek reads 'borders of lawlessness'. The phrase 'angry forever' fits Obadiah's picture of a permanent end for Edom (Obadiah 1:18). Later rabbis used 'Edom' as a code name for Rome, and some Christian writers used it for the church's enemies. Those are later uses, not Malachi's meaning.

p: The Hebrew can mean the LORD is great beyond Israel's land, or great over Israel's land.
b: The Hebrew me'al ligvul Yisra'el literally says 'from over the border of Israel'. Three readings: the LORD's greatness reaches beyond Israel's frontier, so even Edom must see it (the Plain); the LORD is great 'over' Israel's territory, a more local praise; or the LORD is 'magnified' from the border outward. The Latin Vulgate reads 'over the border of Israel'. The first reading prepares the book's turn from Israel to the nations in 1:11 and 1:14, where the name of the LORD is great 'among the nations'.

t: Father, master and the commandment to honor
p: The charge begins with the fifth commandment and two household pictures: a father and a master.
b: Malachi starts from what everyone knows. A son honors his father (Exodus 20:12; Deuteronomy 5:16) and a servant honors his master. The LORD claims both roles. He is Israel's father (Exodus 4:22; Deuteronomy 32:6; Isaiah 63:16; Hosea 11:1) and a master whose servants owe him respect. The word 'honor' (kavod) is the root of 'glory', and 'fear' is the old word for the respect owed a master. The book returns to 'one father' in 2:10 and to a son who serves in 3:17.

p: The first charge is against the Temple priests, who ran the offerings in the Persian province of Judah.
b: After the Temple was rebuilt in about 515 BC, the priests ran its daily offerings (Ezra 6:15-18). Malachi speaks to them directly in 1:6 and 2:1, and the whole of 1:6-2:9 is about their duty. He is not attacking the Temple as Isaiah and Jeremiah sometimes seemed to. He wants it to work as the law says. The charge is that they accept bad animals, treat the altar casually and teach carelessly. 'Priests' here shades into the wider family 'Levi' (2:4-8; 3:3), which is a puzzle (see the note on 2:4).

p: The priests call the altar 'the LORD's table'. The law says the priest who serves it must be holy.
b: The Hebrew word lechem means bread or food. In Leviticus the offerings are 'the food of God' offered by the priests, who must be holy for that reason (Leviticus 21:6; Leviticus 21:21-22). The altar is also called a 'table' (shulchan) in Ezekiel 41:22 and Ezekiel 44:16. The people's excuse in the second half of the verse is that the table is 'despicable' (nivzeh, from the same root idea as the 'despise' of 1:6), and the priests' actions show they believe it. The Plain uses 'despicable' in both 1:7 and 1:12.

p: The law bans blind, lame and sick animals for the altar. Malachi calls it evil without quoting the rule.
b: Leviticus 22:17-25 says an animal for the altar must be flawless (Leviticus 22:21) and lists blind, broken, maimed or diseased animals as unacceptable. Deuteronomy gives the same rule (Deuteronomy 15:21; Deuteronomy 17:1). Malachi assumes the priests know the rule. His argument is not legal but personal: you would not offer such a gift to a governor. The shame is that people in the Persian period evidently gave to God what they would never give a ruler.

p: A Persian provincial governor is expected to receive gifts. The Hebrew word is the one in Haggai.
b: The Hebrew pechah is a foreign loan word, already used in 1 Kings 10:15 and 20:24 ('governors'). In the Persian period it was the usual word for the ruler of a province, used of Zerubbabel (Haggai 1:1) and of Tattenai, governor of the province across the Euphrates (Ezra 5:3). Governors lived off the people and expected gifts, a practice Nehemiah says he gave up (Nehemiah 5:14-18). Malachi does not name the governor. The verse shows only that a Persian-appointed governor was in office, which fits the Persian period and does not date the book more exactly.

p: The Hebrew idiom means to ask for favor. The tone is sharp: go ahead and plead, and see what comes of it.
b: The Hebrew is challu na penei El, 'soften the face of God', an idiom for begging a favor (Exodus 32:11; 1 Samuel 13:12; Zechariah 7:2; Zechariah 8:21-22). Most commentators hear sarcasm: the priests are told to try intercession with these offerings in their hands, and the next question shows how that will go. The 'us' includes the prophet with his people, as in 2:10, where he says 'our ancestors'. A few read the verse as a sincere call to repent, but the lines around it, and 1:10, make that unlikely.

p: The wish is that someone would shut the doors and end the pretend worship. Earlier prophets said much the same.
b: The Hebrew says only 'the doors', which many take as the Temple gates or the doors of the court. The LORD prefers a closed Temple to empty ritual, as earlier prophets said: he hates the festivals (Amos 5:21-22), burnt offerings do not please him when they come from wicked hands (Jeremiah 6:20), and Isaiah 1:11-14 says the same of offerings without justice. Malachi's twist is that the offerings are not only empty, they are bad animals brought to a God who deserves the best.

p: This is the word Leviticus 2, Joel and Amos render 'grain offering'. Here it covers animals too, so the Plain says 'offering'.
b: The Hebrew minchah is the word of Leviticus 2:1, where it is the grain offering, and the site's usual term is 'grain offering' (so the Plain of Joel 1:9, Joel 2:14 and Amos 5:22, 25 and the 'evening grain offering' of Daniel 9:21). The word began as 'gift' or 'tribute' (Genesis 4:3-5, where Abel's animals are a minchah), and 1 Samuel 2:17 uses it for the sacrifices the priests' sons despised. This book uses it widely: the lame and sick animals of 1:13 are brought as a minchah. So the Plain says 'offering' in 1:10, 1:11, 1:13, 2:12, 2:13, 3:3 and 3:4, and keeps 'sacrifice' (zevach) for 1:8 and 1:14. Where the Hebrew does not say what the gift is (2:12, 2:13, 3:3, 3:4), 'offering' leaves it open; it does not claim animals or grain. The Plain of Daniel 9:27 likewise has 'sacrifice and offering'. The cost of the choice is that a reader of Joel and Malachi sees two English words for one Hebrew word. At 1:11 the Hebrew pairs the burning of incense with the minchah, and elsewhere the minchah stands beside frankincense (Jeremiah 17:26; 41:5; Nehemiah 13:5, 9; Isaiah 66:3). That pairing is part of what the next notes discuss.
r: Leviticus 2:1; Genesis 4:3-5; 1 Samuel 2:17; Joel 1:9; Amos 5:22; Daniel 9:21; Daniel 9:27; Jeremiah 17:26; 1:13; 2:12-13; 3:3-4

a: From where the sun rises to where it sets
p: The Hebrew has no verb. The Plain gives the present, the sense most natural for a statement with no verb.
b: The Hebrew says gadol shemi baggoyim, 'great my name among the nations', with no verb of time. Readers have supplied three. Present ('is great'): the LORD's name is already honored among the nations, even when they worship other gods (Rashi's first comment, from the Talmud, Menachot 110a: even a person with an idol knows the God over all gods, and everywhere they give in his name; this fits 'incense is being brought'). Future ('will be great'): Malachi looks to a time when the nations worship him (Isaiah 66:18-21; Zephaniah 3:9-10; Zechariah 14:16). Timeless: the LORD is great wherever he is rightly known. The Greek has 'has been glorified'. The Plain picks the present, as the Hebrew most simply reads; the next note takes up who brings the offering.

a: incense is being burned and brought to my name
t: Who offers it? Jews, nations or the future
p: The incense in every place has been read of Jews abroad, of sincere pagans, of Israel's prayer and Torah study, or of a coming age.
b: Five readings. (1) Jews outside Jerusalem: by the 5th century BC there was a Jewish temple at Elephantine in Egypt that had altars for incense offerings and animal sacrifices, and its leaders wrote to the governor of Judah about rebuilding it (the letter is dated 407 BC). (2) The nations: their worship, even when mistaken, is offered in some sense to the one God (Rashi's first comment, from Menachot 110a). (3) Israel's own worship, wherever it happens: Rashi's second comment gives the Sages' reading that the 'pure offering' is the Torah scholars who study the laws of the Temple service in every place and every prayer of Israel, and he says the Targum Jonathan paraphrases it so. (4) The future: the nations will come to the LORD (Isaiah 66:20; Zephaniah 3:9-10). (5) The church's worship, in the Christian reading (see the next note). The Hebrew has two participles, muqtar muggash, 'incense is being burned, is being presented', and leaves the time open. The incense-and-minchah pair is one the Temple used (see the note at 1:10).

p: From the Didache onward, many Christians read this verse of the Eucharist. Others read it differently.
b: The earliest witnesses are the Didache (14:1-3), which quotes the verse for the Lord's Day thanksgiving, Justin Martyr (Dialogue with Trypho 41 and 117) and Irenaeus (Against Heresies 4.17.5 to 4.18.1). The Council of Trent (Session 22, chapter 1) and the Catechism of the Catholic Church (1350) cite the verse for the Mass as the offering of the new covenant. The Reformers answered that the verse speaks of the spread of true worship, prayer and praise among the nations, and not of a repeated sacrifice of Christ (see the card). The Jewish readings are in the previous notes. The Latin Vulgate has in omni loco sacrificatur et offertur nomini meo oblatio munda, 'in every place a sacrifice is made and an offering presented to my name, a clean offering', which turns the Hebrew incense into sacrifice and is the wording these readers lean on; the Hebrew and the Greek have incense. The Plain leaves the phrase literal: an offering that is tehorah, 'clean'.

a: turn up your nose at it
p: The verb means to puff or blow, a gesture of scorn. Some old lists of scribal 'softenings' include this verse.
b: The verb hippachtem is from puach, 'to blow': to puff in contempt. The Mekhilta of Rabbi Ishmael lists this verse among passages where Scripture speaks euphemistically: it says the text is actually written 'Him'. It is one of the places called Tiqqune Sopherim (the 'scribal corrections', a tradition that scribes softened a few lines that spoke too boldly about God), where the original may have read 'at me' instead of 'at it'. The evidence is a tradition about the text, not a manuscript with the other reading,. The Greek of this verse differs more widely: it has the people say 'These things come from hardship', and then the LORD says 'and I blew on them' (exephysesa), with God as the one who blows (see the variant). The Plain follows the Hebrew we have.

p: The word means taken by force. Isaiah says the LORD hates robbery in a burnt offering.
b: The Hebrew gazul means seized or taken by force, perhaps stolen goods or an animal taken from another man. Isaiah 61:8 says the LORD loves justice and hates robbery in the burnt offering. Leviticus assumes an offering is the worshiper's own (Leviticus 1:3-4). Some commentators suggest 'torn' (by a beast), since the law forbids such meat (Leviticus 17:15), but the Hebrew word is the one for robbery.

t: A vow and a bad animal
p: A man vows a good male, then pays with a ruined one. The law treats a vow as a debt to the LORD.
b: The vow was voluntary but binding once spoken (Deuteronomy 23:21-23; Numbers 30:2). A male was the standard burnt offering (Leviticus 1:3), and an animal with a defect would not do (Leviticus 22:18-21). The word 'spoiled' is mashchat, from the root 'to ruin', and Leviticus 22:25 uses the same root of an animal with a defect. The 'swindler' (nokhel) is one who deals deceptively; the root is rare, and it appears elsewhere in Numbers 25:18 of the Midianites' scheme at Peor.

p: 'Great king' was a Persian royal title and also older treaty language. Whether Malachi echoes it is a reading.
b: In Persian royal inscriptions the ruler calls himself 'the great king, king of kings', and in earlier treaties the 'great king' is the overlord whose vassals owe him tribute. The same phrase is used of the LORD without any Persian setting (Psalm 47:2; Psalm 95:3). Malachi has already told the priests to take their bad gifts to the governor (1:8). One view hears the LORD claiming the title of the Persian ruler above the governor of 1:8; this is an inference, since the verse does not mention Persia, and the psalms and treaty language explain the phrase without it. Either way the claim fits the book's theme: the God of Israel is not one local deity, and the nations fear his name.

a: put a curse on your blessings
p: Priests pronounced the blessing of Numbers 6. Their own blessings, or the blessings they receive, are cursed.
b: The Hebrew ve-'arothi 'et-birkhoteikhem can mean the blessings the priests pronounce on the people (the blessing of Numbers 6:22-27), or the blessings the priests themselves receive: the good harvests and shares of offerings. Both are possible. 'The curse' (with the article) points back to the covenant curses of Deuteronomy 28:15-20, which come with the blessings of Deuteronomy 28:1-14. Malachi 3:9 uses the same word for the whole nation: 'You are cursed with the curse.' The same covenant pattern of reward and penalty runs through Haggai 1:6-11, where drought answers neglect of the Temple.

p: The 'dung' is the stomach contents of sacrificed animals, burned outside the camp because it was unclean.
b: The Hebrew peresh is the contents of an animal's stomach and intestines, which the law ordered burned outside the camp with the hide (Exodus 29:14; Leviticus 4:11-12; Leviticus 16:27). To have it smeared on the face is the opposite of the priestly consecration: the priest is cast out with the waste. 'Your festivals' means the festival sacrifices the priests had offered. The Jerusalem 'Dung Gate' (Nehemiah 2:13; Nehemiah 12:31) may be named from where such waste left the city. 'Carried off with it' means to be taken out to the dung heap along with it.

p: No law text names it. It draws on Deuteronomy 33, the golden calf story and Phinehas.
b: No passage in the Pentateuch uses the exact phrase 'covenant with Levi'. The nearest are the blessing of Levi (Deuteronomy 33:8-11), the Levites' zeal after the golden calf (Exodus 32:26-29) and the LORD's covenant of peace with Phinehas: "Look, I am giving him my covenant: peace." (Numbers 25:12). Jeremiah speaks of a covenant with the Levitical priests (Jeremiah 33:17-22), and Nehemiah 13:29 speaks of 'the covenant of the priesthood and of the Levites'. Malachi's 'life and peace' (2:5) echoes Numbers 25:12. Scholars debate whether Malachi, like Deuteronomy, treats all Levites as priests (the 'Levite priests') or reflects a conflict between priests and Levites; Julia O'Brien wrote a book-length study with the title Priest and Levite in Malachi (1990).

p: Here 'teaching' is the priests' spoken instruction. The same word names the whole law of Moses in 4:4.
b: The Hebrew torah means instruction. In priestly speech it is the ruling a priest gives, on what is clean and unclean or what the law requires (Leviticus 10:10-11; Deuteronomy 33:10; Haggai 2:11-13, where Haggai asks the priests for a ruling). So 'true teaching' (torat emet) is a priest's reliable answer, and 2:7 says people go to his mouth for it. The Plain uses 'teaching' in 2:6-9 and 'law' in 4:4, where the word means the law of Moses. Malachi accuses the priests of exactly what Ezekiel and Zephaniah accused earlier priests of (Ezekiel 22:26; Zephaniah 3:4).

a: the messenger of the LORD of Armies
t: A priest as the LORD's messenger
p: This is the only place a priest is called the LORD's messenger. The same word is Malachi's name and 3:1.
b: The Hebrew mal'akh YHWH tseva'ot is the title of a divine messenger or angel in other places, and Haggai is called "the LORD's messenger" in the Plain (Haggai 1:13). Here it is a priest, who carries the LORD's word to the people as a prophet or an angel does. The idea ties the book together: Malachi's own name or title ('my messenger', 1:1), the priest as messenger (2:7), the coming messenger who clears the road (3:1) and the messenger of the covenant (3:1). The charge in 2:8 is that the priests have stopped being what 2:7 says a priest is.

p: The Hebrew idiom 'lift faces' means to show favor. It is the same idiom as 'receive you kindly' in 1:8-9.
b: The Hebrew nos'im panim ('lifting faces') is the idiom for showing partiality, and the law forbids it for judges (Leviticus 19:15; Deuteronomy 1:17). It is the same idiom, in a different sense, as in 1:8 and 1:9: 'receive you kindly' is literally 'lift your face'. The priests who will not 'lift the face' of the LORD (they offer him less than they would give a governor) are now said to 'lift faces' in their teaching, favoring some people over others. The LORD pays them back in kind: he has made them low before all the people.

p: Is it the LORD, Abraham or a common human ancestor? The parallel line 'one God created us' points to the LORD.
b: Three readings. (1) The LORD, who is Israel's father (1:6; Isaiah 63:16; Deuteronomy 32:6). This fits the parallel line, 'one God created us', and is the most common view. (2) Abraham or Jacob, the father of the nation (Isaiah 51:2); in this view the people share one ancestor, and the 'one God' made the nation. (3) A universal sense, all human beings sharing one creator. The question is the ground of the argument that follows: if we have one father, we owe each other loyalty. 'Betray' in the same verse introduces the word that runs through 2:10-16.

p: One Hebrew verb is used five times in these seven verses.
b: The Hebrew bagad means to act treacherously, to break faith with a person to whom one owes loyalty. It appears five times, in 2:10, 2:11, 2:14, 2:15 and 2:16, and the Plain always says 'betray'. The verb is used of unfaithful marriage (Jeremiah 3:20; Jeremiah 12:6) and of covenant disloyalty. The repeated verb makes marriage and covenant one subject: betraying a brother, the wife of one's youth and the LORD's holy place are all the same sin.

a: the daughter of a foreign god
t: Marriage to a foreign god's daughter
p: Is it literal intermarriage with foreign women, or a picture of Judah's turning to other gods?
b: The Hebrew bat el nekhar is literally 'the daughter of a foreign god'. Three readings. (1) Literal: Judean men married women of other peoples who worshiped other gods, as Ezra 9-10 and Nehemiah 13:23-27 describe. Nehemiah 13:23 in the Plain: "In those days, too, I saw Jews who had taken Ashdodite, Ammonite and Moabite women into their homes." (2) Figurative: Judah, as a whole, has taken a foreign god as a partner, a picture of idolatry. (3) A combination: some Judean men divorced their Judean wives to marry foreign women (2:13-16 is then the same scandal). Each view has to explain how 2:11 fits 2:14-16, and whether Malachi agrees with the solution in Ezra 10, where the foreign wives are sent away.

p: The Hebrew 'one who wakes and one who answers' is unclear. It may mean 'everyone' or 'teacher and pupil'.
b: The Hebrew 'er ve-'oneh is a rare pair. Proposals: an idiom meaning 'every last one' (those awake and those answering, as in a watch); a pair of persons, such as 'the teacher and the pupil' (the Latin Vulgate has magistrum et discipulum); or a text damaged in copying. The scroll 4QXIIa (4Q76) reads 'witness' ('ed), with a different last consonant, and the Greek has 'until he is humbled'. See the variant. The verse's point is plain even if the pair is not: the offender is cut off from the community of Jacob's tents, whatever his rank or his offerings.

a: cover the altar of the LORD with tears
p: The tears may be the men's own over rejected offerings, or the divorced wives' weeping at the altar.
b: The Hebrew says 'you do' this, so the plain reading is that the men themselves cover the altar with tears and groans because their offerings are not accepted. A second view, found already in the Talmud, hears the abandoned wives behind the tears: it says that when a man divorces his first wife, even the altar sheds tears over him (Gittin 90b). A third reading takes the weeping as mourning rites that go with fasting (compare Joel 2:12-17). The ties to 2:14 ('the wife of your youth') make the second view natural, but the verse does not say the wives are weeping.

p: 'Wife of your covenant' treats marriage itself as a covenant, with the LORD as witness.
b: The Hebrew 'eshet ne'urekha ('the wife of your youth') is the phrase of Proverbs 5:18, and 'wife of your covenant' ('eshet beritekha) treats marriage as a covenant (compare Proverbs 2:16-17 and Ezekiel 16:8). Gordon Hugenberger's study of marriage as a covenant is developed 'from the perspective of Malachi' (the subtitle of his book). Others read 'covenant' here as the covenant at Sinai that binds all Israel, and see the wife as a symbol of the people. The passage can carry both: the same verb 'betray' covers disloyalty to a wife and to the covenant. Whether the 'witness' is a legal oath or a general moral presence is not clear.

a: Did he not make one? A remnant of spirit was his.
t: The hardest verse in the book
p: The Hebrew is broken or very compressed. No reading is sure. The Plain stays close to the Hebrew words.
b: Every word of 2:15 is disputed. The Plain translates what the Hebrew says and leaves the sense open. Main readings of 'Did he not make one?': (1) God made husband and wife one (compare Genesis 2:24), with a share of his spirit given to them. (2) The 'one' is the husband: Rashi, following the sense of the Targum Jonathan, reads 'what does the one seek?' of a husband who looks for grounds against his wife, who is the 'seed of God', and corrects the Targum's punctuation. He then gives a second explanation, an exchange about one who 'had a different spirit', did not cast his eye on another woman, and sought 'seed of God'. (3) The 'one' is Abraham, the single father of the nation (compare Isaiah 51:2); Rashi does not read it so. (4) The 'one' is the one God, who made a single pair. (5) The Greek and some scholars read a different text altogether (see the variant). 'Offspring from God' (zera' 'Elohim) is read as 'godly children', raised in the covenant, or as 'children God desired'. The verse ends in a command that is clear: guard yourselves, and do not betray the wife of your youth.

t: 'He hates sending away': who is speaking, and what is hated?
p: The Hebrew can say the LORD hates divorce, or that a man who hates his wife may send her away. Rashi and the Targum read it the second way.
b: The Hebrew ki sane' shallach has four readings. (1) 'For he hates sending away' (the Plain). (2) 'I hate divorce' (sane' read as 'I hate'); the speaker is then the LORD. (3) 'If you hate her, send her away': the reading of the Greek, the Vulgate, Rashi and the Targum Jonathan. Rashi sends the reader to the dispute in Gittin 90b, and the Dead Sea scroll 4QXIIa visibly has 'if', 'hate' and 'send away' and no more (see the variant). So the main line of Jewish exegesis takes the verse as a permission with a warning, not as 'God hates divorce'. (4) 'The man who hates and sends away', as in some modern versions. Sane' also means 'unloved' of a wife (Deuteronomy 21:15; 24:3), and shallach is the verb of Deuteronomy 24:1-3. The Plain takes 'covering one's garment with violence' as a second thing hated, parallel to 'sending away'; the next note gives other choices. Jesus: "Moses let you divorce your wives in view of your hard-heartedness. But from the beginning it has not been that way." (Matthew 19:8). He answers from Genesis and Deuteronomy 24, not Malachi. See the card.

p: Spreading a garment over a woman meant marriage and protection. Violence on the garment is a crime against that bond.
b: In Hebrew marriage language, a man spreads his garment (or the corner of it) over a woman as a sign of protection and claim (Ruth 3:9; Ezekiel 16:8; Deuteronomy 22:30). 'Covering his garment with violence' is read three ways: the man's marriage-cloak is now a cover for harm; the violence is visible as a stain on his clothes, as bloodstains would be; or the garment stands for the wife, so the verse says violence covers her. The Greek reads 'ungodliness will cover your thoughts', a different Hebrew reading (see the variant). The Hebrew word here is levush, 'clothing', not the common beged.

a: Where is the God of justice?
p: The people ask what Habakkuk, Jeremiah and the psalmists asked: why do the wicked do well?
b: The Hebrew 'ayeh 'Elohei ha-mishpat asks where the God who judges is. It is the old question of the righteous sufferer: Jeremiah 12:1, Habakkuk 1:2-4 and 1:13, Psalm 73, Job 21. Malachi gives a different cast to it. The people who ask are the same ones the LORD charges with evil (1:6-2:16), and the first part of the saying ('everyone who does evil is good in the LORD's eyes') is nearer to cynicism than to grief. The answer in 3:1-5 is that the God of justice is coming, and the people who ask will not be able to stand. The question returns in 3:14-15.

p: A forerunner, Elijah, an angel, a priest or Malachi himself: the book leaves the figure open until 4:5.
b: The Hebrew mal'akhi is the word that is the book's title (1:1), the priest in 2:7, and here a figure who clears the road. Views. (1) A human forerunner whom the LORD sends before his own coming, later identified with Elijah (4:5); this is how Matthew 11:10-14 and the other Gospels read it. (2) An angel, like the angel of Exodus 23:20. (3) The prophet himself, if 'Malachi' is a title taken from this verse. (4) A priest, from 2:7. Many Jewish commentators join 3:1 to 4:5 and name Elijah. The Plain keeps the same English, 'messenger', in 1:1, 2:7 and 3:1, so the reader can see the link; only the Hebrew can say which meaning is on top.

p: The Gospels quote the verse and the Greek differs: 'before you', not 'before me', and it blends with Exodus 23:20.
b: Matthew and Luke quote the verse with words from both Malachi and Exodus: "Look, I am sending my messenger before your face. He will make your road ready ahead of you." (Matthew 11:10; Luke 7:27). The Hebrew of Malachi says 'before me'; the Greek form says 'before your face' and 'your road', which is the wording of Exodus 23:20 in the Greek: "Here, I am sending an angel in front of you to keep you safe on the way and to bring you into the place I have made ready." (Exodus 23:20). So in the Gospels the speaker addresses the one who comes, and the messenger goes before that person's face, not before the LORD's. Mark joins the same blend to Isaiah 40:3 and introduces both with "Just as it stands written in Isaiah the prophet" (Mark 1:2). The Byzantine text and the Textus Receptus (and so the KJV) do not have 'in Isaiah the prophet' but 'in the prophets', a likely smoothing of the same difficulty.

a: the Lord you are looking for
t: The Lord comes to his temple
p: 'The Lord' here is the LORD himself. His return to his temple answers a hope from Ezekiel.
b: The Hebrew ha-'adon, 'the Lord' (with the article), is used of the LORD himself elsewhere, as in Isaiah 1:24 and Isaiah 3:1, so the Plain capitalizes it. 'His temple' is the LORD's own. The people ask in 2:17 where the God of justice is, and he answers that he is coming to the Temple that was rebuilt in about 515 BC. Ezekiel had seen his glory leave the first Temple (Ezekiel 10:18-19) and had been shown it returning to a restored Temple in a vision (Ezekiel 43:1-5); that Temple of Ezekiel 40-48 is not the one finished in about 515 BC. Malachi's hearers could take Ezekiel's promise as still unfulfilled. Haggai and Zechariah had said the Temple would be filled with his presence (Haggai 2:7-9; Zechariah 2:10-12). The irony of 3:1-2 is that those who seek him cannot bear his coming.

p: These words occur only here. The figure is the LORD's agent for judgment and purification.
b: The Hebrew mal'akh ha-berit, 'messenger of the covenant', occurs only here. Which covenant? The covenant with Levi (2:4-8), the covenant of Sinai or an eschatological covenant. Views on who he is: the same person as 'the Lord' in the same verse (the two lines are parallel); a separate figure who carries out the LORD's judgment (the angel of Exodus 23:20-23); the forerunner of 3:1a; Elijah (4:5); or a priest-like figure who purifies Levi in 3:3. Christian readers see Christ, or John the Baptist and Christ together. The Plain says 'whom you delight in', the people's word for him, which 3:2 immediately questions.

a: the soap of those who wash clothes
p: Two pictures of cleansing by something harsh: melting metal, and scrubbing cloth with lye.
b: A refiner melts silver or gold in a furnace to burn off the dross (Isaiah 1:25; Jeremiah 6:27-30; Ezekiel 22:17-22; Zechariah 13:9). The Hebrew borit, here 'soap', is a strong alkali, used by cloth-washers (fullers) who trampled and scrubbed wool (Jeremiah 2:22). The fuller's field was outside Jerusalem (Isaiah 7:3). The two pictures answer 'who can live through it?': the fire is harsh because it is for cleansing. Handel's Messiah sets the verse for a bass voice ("But who may abide the day of his coming", in the King James wording of Charles Jennens's libretto), and that is where many English readers meet it; the music is a reception, not a reading of Malachi.

t: A list from the covenant law
p: The sins in 3:5 follow the old laws. The foreigner is protected here, though 2:11 condemned marrying foreigners.
b: The list is a short summary of the covenant law: sorcery (Exodus 22:18), adultery (Exodus 20:14; Leviticus 20:10), false oaths (Exodus 20:7; Leviticus 19:12), cheating a day laborer of his wages (Leviticus 19:13; Deuteronomy 24:14-15), and wronging the widow, the fatherless and the foreigner (Exodus 22:21-24; Deuteronomy 24:17-22). The widow, orphan and foreigner are the three groups Deuteronomy asks Israel to look after. The Greek calls the last one a 'proselyte' (prosēlytos). Some readers see a conflict with the ban on foreign marriages in 2:11; most commentators answer that the two concern different things: 2:11 is about worship and the marriage of a Judean to a woman of another faith, and 3:5 is about justice to a resident foreigner.

p: The LORD's constancy explains why Jacob's family survives. It does not mean he cannot change his mind about harm.
b: The Hebrew verb is shanah, 'to change'. The point is God's loyalty to his covenant: because he does not change, the people of Jacob have not been wiped out. This does not conflict with passages where the LORD 'changes his mind' about a threatened harm, which use another verb, nacham: "...one who changes his mind about the harm." (Jonah 4:2). The two ideas are in the same creed (Exodus 34:6-7, which Jonah quotes). The constancy is moral, in his purposes, and the mercy is the proof. Numbers 23:19 and 1 Samuel 15:29 say similar things of God, and James 1:17 speaks of the 'Father of lights' with no change or shadow.

a: Return to me, and I will return to you
p: The same sentence opens Zechariah, and the prophets ask 'return' again and again. It is the word of repentance.
b: The Hebrew shuvu 'elai ve-'ashuvah 'alekhem is almost the same as Zechariah 1:3, the first message of the book that comes just before Malachi in the Twelve. The Chronicler's Hezekiah says something close: if the people return to the LORD, he will not turn his face from them (2 Chronicles 30:9). 'Return' (shuv) is the Hebrew word for repentance, a turning around, and Jeremiah and Hosea use it often (Jeremiah 3:12-14; Hosea 14:1-2; Joel 2:12-13). The people's answer, 'How are we to return?', is the book's most honest question: they do not know what they did wrong, and the next verse tells them.

p: The law set a tenth for the Levites and a share for the priests. Malachi says the people have kept them back.
b: The tithe (ma'aser, 'tenth') of grain, fruit and animals belonged to the LORD and was given to the Levites (Leviticus 27:30-32; Numbers 18:21-24); they gave a tenth of it to the priests (Numbers 18:25-32). Deuteronomy asks the people to eat a tithe at the sanctuary and to give a tithe every third year for the poor and the Levites (Deuteronomy 14:22-29). The 'contribution' (terumah) is the priests' share of the offerings and first fruits. Jewish tradition later counted several tithes (first tithe, second tithe, poor tithe); Tobit 1:6-8 and Josephus describe such a system (Antiquities 4.8.22). Critical scholars think the law developed in stages, and that the commands of Numbers, Deuteronomy and Leviticus did not originally describe one system. Nehemiah 10:37-39 and 13:10-13 show what the Persian-period community promised and what it did.
r: Leviticus 27:30-32; Numbers 18:21-32; Deuteronomy 14:22-29; Nehemiah 10:37-39; Nehemiah 13:10-13; Tobit 1:6-8

t: Claude's theory: Jacob, the supplanter, and the word 'rob'
p: The rare verb for 'rob' sounds like Jacob's name, and the Greek chose the verb used of Jacob.
b: The Hebrew verb qava' ('rob', here only in this verse and Proverbs 22:23) uses the same three consonants as 'aqav ('to trip up, to supplant') in a different order, and 'aqav is the verb behind Jacob's name (Genesis 27:36; Hosea 12:3). The Greek translator renders qava' with pternizō, 'to trip up, to supplant', the verb the Septuagint uses at Genesis 27:36 for what Jacob did to Esau. In 3:6 the people are called 'sons of Jacob', and the book opened with 'Jacob I loved' (1:2). My theory is that the audience hears 'sons of Jacob ... you are tripping up' as a charge: you have become the old Jacob, taking what is not yours. This is mine. I do not know whether anyone has proposed the letter-link in print; the Greek verb only shows that an ancient translator read the word that way.

a: You are cursed with the curse
t: Malachi 3:9-10 in the scroll and the Greek
p: A Dead Sea scroll reads the start of 3:9 differently, and the Greek has a very different text of 3:9-10.
b: The Hebrew ba-me'erah 'attem ne'arim ('with the curse you are cursed') uses the noun and verb of the same root, as in 2:2. The Dead Sea scroll 4QXIIa (4Q76) begins the verse with different letters (umar'im) and then has a restored word, so its reading cannot be made out with confidence; the printout marks the difference and the transcription is partly restored. The Greek has a longer, different text: 'You look and look, and you trip me up; the year is finished, and you have brought all the produce into the treasuries.' The Plain follows the Hebrew; the Greek looks like a loose retelling, though it may rest on another Hebrew form.

p: Nehemiah 13 describes the same storehouses: empty when the Levites went back to their fields.
b: The Hebrew beit ha-'otsar is the Temple's treasury or store, with its chambers for tithes of grain, wine and oil (Nehemiah 10:37-39; 1 Chronicles 26:20; 2 Chronicles 31:11-12). Nehemiah says that when he came back to Jerusalem for a second term, a large room that had held the tithes had been given to Tobiah (Nehemiah 13:4-9), no one had been handing the Levites their shares, and the Levites and singers "had run off to his own field" (Nehemiah 13:10). After Nehemiah acted, "All Judah now brought in the tithe of grain, new wine and olive oil to the storehouses." (Nehemiah 13:12). The match is close, and many scholars set Malachi near Nehemiah's second term (about 432 BC) or just before it. The date is argued: Malachi never names Nehemiah, the abuse may have happened more than once, and Nehemiah's report may have been written after Malachi or before.

p: The image is rain from the sky. Genesis uses it for the Flood, and Elisha's story uses it for a sudden harvest.
b: The Hebrew 'arubbot ha-shamayim ('windows' or 'sluices' of the heavens) appears in Genesis 7:11 and Genesis 8:2 for the Flood, and in 2 Kings 7:2 and 7:19 for an impossible gift of grain, where an officer says 'if the LORD made windows in the heavens'. In Malachi it is a blessing of rain and harvest, after the drought and blight that Haggai describes (Haggai 1:10-11; 2:16-17); Joel's locusts are not dated and may belong to another time. The image fits the farmer's world: when the sky opens, the crops come. Whether the blessing is only grain, or also other kinds of wealth, is not said; 3:11-12 speak of the harvest and the land.

t: Testing God, and a popular misuse
p: The same verb in 3:15 is what evildoers do to God. Here the LORD invites it, once. It is not a rule for investing money.
b: The Hebrew bachan, 'to test', is usually forbidden toward God (Deuteronomy 6:16; Psalm 95:8-9). Here the LORD himself invites the test, and the same verb in 3:15 describes the wicked who 'test God' and escape. The difference is the setting: Malachi addresses the whole community in a covenant crisis (the verbs are plural, and 3:9 says 'the whole nation'), and the 'blessing' (3:10-12) is rain, crops and an end to the devourer. A popular use of the verse, in the teaching often called the prosperity gospel, makes it a promise that gifts to a ministry will return as money to the individual giver. The text does not say that: it promises harvests to a community that returns to its covenant duty, and its 'storehouse' fed the Levites and priests.

p: 'The devourer' is a crop pest such as the locust, one of the old covenant curses. Haggai describes failed harvests in the same years.
b: The Hebrew ha-'okhel is a plain participle, 'the eater'. It names no animal; the sense is a crop pest such as the locust (Joel 1:4 uses four other words for the locust's stages) or the pests of Deuteronomy 28:38-42, listed there among the covenant curses. Amos 4:9 says the LORD sent locusts that devoured the gardens, and Haggai 1:10-11 and 2:16-17 describe blight and drought in the years before the Temple was rebuilt. The LORD promises to 'rebuke' the devourer, the verb used for rebuking the sea or a hostile power (Psalm 106:9; Nahum 1:4). A promise of freedom from the devourer is the reverse of the curse of 2:2 and 3:9.

p: Isaiah gave Zion the name 'My Delight Is in Her'. Malachi says the nations will see Judah that way.
b: The Hebrew 'eretz chefets ('land of delight') recalls Isaiah 62:4, where Zion is renamed 'My Delight Is in Her' (Hephzibah) and the land 'Married', a promise to the returning exiles. Zechariah 7:14 had said the pleasant land was made desolate; Malachi says the nations will call it happy. 'Call you happy' ('ishshru) comes from the same root as 'blessed is the one' of the psalms, 'ashrei. In 3:15 the speakers call the proud 'happy' with the same verb, so the book sets two blessings side by side.

p: Job's friends, Job and a psalmist all voice this complaint. Here it is a quoted saying of the people.
b: The Hebrew shav' ('worthless', 'empty') is the word of the third commandment ('in vain'). The complaint is old: Job 21:14-15, Job 34:9 and Psalm 73:13, where the poet says that keeping his heart clean was pointless. Two of its words belong to the priest's job: 'keeping his charge' (mishmeret) is the priests' and Levites' watch (Numbers 18:5), and the 'gloom' is the dark garb or look of fasting and mourning (Psalm 35:14; Psalm 38:6). So the people claim they have kept the LORD's rules in a priestly way and have nothing to show for it. The answer is the scroll of remembrance in 3:16-18.

p: Persian kings kept records of those who served them; the Bible has heavenly books too.
b: The Hebrew sefer zikkaron is a record kept 'before him'. At the Persian court, a record of memorable deeds was read to the king (Esther 6:1-3), and Greek historians report that the Persian king's scribes wrote down the names of his benefactors (for example Herodotus, Histories 8.85-90). The Bible speaks of heavenly records: the LORD's book (Exodus 32:32-33), the tally of tears (Psalm 56:8), the book of the living (Psalm 69:28), the books of Daniel 7:10 and Daniel 12:1, and the books of Revelation 20:12. Nehemiah prays 'remember me' again and again (Nehemiah 13:14, 22, 31). The record here is for those who fear the LORD, so the reader knows God has heard.
r: Exodus 32:32-33; Psalm 56:8; Psalm 69:28; Daniel 7:10; Daniel 12:1; Esther 6:1-3; Nehemiah 13:31; Revelation 20:12

p: The word is the one used of all Israel at Sinai. Here it names the faithful inside Israel.
b: The Hebrew segullah is a king's personal treasure, apart from the state's wealth (1 Chronicles 29:3; Ecclesiastes 2:8). At Sinai the LORD called all Israel his segullah (Exodus 19:5; Deuteronomy 7:6; Deuteronomy 14:2). Malachi gives the title to those who fear the LORD, the people who spoke in 3:16, and distinguishes them from the wicked in 3:18. This is a quiet form of the remnant idea: not all who belong to the nation belong to the treasure. Titus 2:14 and 1 Peter 2:9 apply the word to the church. The phrase 'the day when I act' also opens 4:3.

a: a man has compassion on his son who serves him
p: The picture is Psalm 103:13, with a twist: the son 'serves' the father, as the people said service was pointless.
b: The comparison to a father's pity echoes Psalm 103:13. The word 'serves' ('avad) is the Hebrew for both a son's work for his father and Israel's service of the LORD, and it appears four times: in 3:14, in 3:17 and twice in 3:18. In 3:14 the people said that serving God was pointless; in 3:17 the LORD says a father has compassion on a son who serves him. The son-servant is the model of Malachi's relationship from 1:6, where the son honors his father and a servant honors his master. The two roles are joined in the faithful.

a: For look, the day is coming
p: The Hebrew Bible has three chapters. English splits the last six verses off as chapter 4.
b: English Bibles follow the chapter division of the Latin Vulgate and begin a fourth chapter at what the Hebrew calls 3:19. So English 4:1-6 is Hebrew 3:19-24, and Hebrew Malachi has 3 chapters, the last with 24 verses. This site uses the English numbers. The Leningrad Codex marks a small paragraph break (a setumah) at the end of Hebrew 3:18, but the thought runs on from the sorting of the righteous and the wicked to the day that does it, so the chapter split is a convenience for reading. The Greek (Swete's text) divides a little differently: its chapter 4 begins one clause earlier than the Latin and English, with the last words of English 3:18 ('and of the one who does not serve'), and its 4:4-6 are English 4:5, 4:6 and 4:4, because the Greek puts the verse on Moses last.

p: The oven that burns the proud is also the picture Obadiah uses for Esau's house, in the same word.
b: The Hebrew tannur is a baking oven (Hosea 7:4-7; Leviticus 26:26) and the heat of a furnace in judgment (Psalm 21:9). The wicked will be qash, 'stubble', the same word Obadiah uses: "the house of Esau stubble" (Obadiah 1:18). Obadiah's picture is Jacob as fire and Esau as stubble, and Malachi has already spoken of Esau in 1:2-5, so the echo is likely meant: what was said of Edom is now said of every proud person and evildoer, in Israel too. 'Neither root nor branch' is a stock expression of total destruction (Amos 2:9; Job 18:16).

a: a sun of righteousness will rise
p: No article: 'a sun', not 'the Sun'. The Hebrew points to the LORD's saving justice rising like a dawn.
b: The Hebrew shemesh tsedaqah ('a sun of righteousness') has no article. Readings. (1) The LORD's righteous salvation coming as the dawn, which burns the wicked (4:1) and heals the righteous. The Talmud pictures this: in the age to come the sun burns the wicked and heals the righteous (Avodah Zarah 3b-4a, quoting this passage). The LORD himself is called 'sun and shield' in Psalm 84:11, and Isaiah 58:8 and 60:1-3 use dawn and light for his help. (2) The Messiah. This is the common Christian reading from the early church on: Jerome and Calvin take the sun as Christ, and Zechariah's father speaks of "the Dawn from on high" (Luke 1:78). (3) Righteousness itself, as vindication. The Plain says 'a sun' and leaves the choice open. The Christian reading is a reception, a fitting one, but not what the Hebrew says by itself.

p: Winged sun discs were common symbols in Egypt, Mesopotamia and Persia. Malachi's image may use one, without worship.
b: Ancient Near Eastern art often shows the sun as a winged disc: Egypt's Horus of Behdet, Assyrian and Persian royal symbols, and the winged disc over the figure on the Persian rock relief at Behistun, in the rule of the kings under whom Malachi lived. The sun god of Mesopotamia, Shamash, was also the god of justice. It is possible that Malachi's image of a sun with 'wings' of healing borrows from this common picture, as a sign that the LORD, not a sun god, brings justice and healing. The link is not proven: the Hebrew kanaf ('wing', 'corner') is also used of the wings of a bird or a garment's corner, and no Hebrew text calls the sun a god. Verdict: a likely background image, no worship.

a: Remember the law of Moses my servant
t: Moses and Elijah at the end of the Prophets
p: These three verses close the Twelve and, in the Hebrew Bible, the Prophets. They look back to Deuteronomy.
b: The closing words join the Law and the Prophets. 'Horeb', 'rules and rulings' and 'all Israel' are the language of Deuteronomy (Deuteronomy 4:1-5; Deuteronomy 5:1-3). The Torah ends by saying no prophet since has been like Moses (Deuteronomy 34:10-12), after promising "a prophet like me" (Deuteronomy 18:15); the Prophets end with Elijah, a prophet who also went to Horeb (1 Kings 19:8). Some read 4:4-6 as an editor's closing note to the Twelve, or to the whole Prophets, and some think it a later addition, since it moves from the book's disputes to a general summary. In Protestant and most Catholic Bibles Malachi is the last book of the Old Testament, and Matthew follows. In the Hebrew Bible the Prophets are followed by the Writings.

a: I am about to send you
p: Elijah was taken up in a whirlwind (2 Kings 2:11), so Judaism expected him back. The New Testament names John.
b: Elijah never died (2 Kings 2:11), so a return fit the story. Ben Sira says he was 'destined' to come back to calm God's anger and to restore Jacob's tribes (Sirach 48:10). The Mishnah says Elijah will come to settle disputes and bring peace, quoting this verse (Eduyot 8:7), and Jewish custom keeps a place for him at the Passover meal (a custom attested in later centuries). In the New Testament, people ask whether John or Jesus is Elijah (John 1:21; Mark 8:28). Jesus says: "And if you are ready to receive it, John himself is Elijah, the one who was going to come." (Matthew 11:14), and later: "Elijah came already." (Matthew 17:12). Luke's angel says John will go ahead of the Lord "with Elijah's spirit and power" (Luke 1:17), which is closer to 'in the role of' than 'in person'. John himself says: "I am not." (John 1:21).
r: 2 Kings 2:11; Sirach 48:10; Matthew 11:14; Matthew 17:10-13; Mark 9:11-13; Luke 1:17; John 1:21

p: The same two words describe the day in Joel. Joel and Malachi frame the Twelve's talk of the day of the LORD.
b: The Hebrew gadol ve-nora' is the phrase of Joel 2:31: "...before the day of the LORD arrives, that great and awesome day." (Joel 2:31). Joel 2:11 says the same of the day. The Greek of Malachi has 'great and clear' (epiphanē), the word Acts 2:20 uses for Joel's day in Peter's quotation. The day of the LORD runs through the Twelve (Amos 5:18-20; Zephaniah 1:14-18; Zechariah 14) and it ends here with a warning and a messenger sent ahead of it. The Plain uses the same English in Joel and Malachi so the reader can see the link.
r: Joel 2:11; Joel 2:31; Amos 5:18-20; Zephaniah 1:14-18; Zechariah 14:1; Acts 2:20

a: turn the hearts of fathers back to their sons
p: Family peace, or generations returning to the covenant? Luke 1:17 reads it as family and as repentance.
b: The Hebrew ve-heshiv lev 'avot 'al banim ('and he will turn back the heart of fathers to sons') has three readings. (1) Families reconciled: fathers and sons turn to each other, ending quarrels, and in Mishnah Eduyot 8:7 the Elijah of peace. (2) Generations reunited around the covenant: sons return to the faith of the fathers, or fathers repent and teach their sons. (3) A national turning in the days of the mixed marriages and divorces of 2:10-16, since children's welfare is in view in 2:15. The Greek reads 'the heart of a man to his neighbor'. In the Gospel, the angel says John "will turn fathers' hearts back to their children, and bring the disobedient around to the good sense of the righteous" (Luke 1:17), which explains the turn as repentance. The Greek verb is 'will restore' (apokatastesei), with a singular 'heart of a father to a son'; see the variant, and Matthew 17:11.

t: The ban, and the last word of the Hebrew
p: The Hebrew ends on 'ban' (cherem). In Jewish reading practice the previous verse is repeated to end on a better note.
b: The Hebrew cherem is total devotion to destruction (Deuteronomy 7:2; Deuteronomy 13:15-17; Joshua 6:17). The threat is that the LORD himself will do to the land what Israel was told to do to the Canaanites if the turning does not come. The Jewish custom of the public reading is to repeat the next-to-last verse (Hebrew 3:23, English 4:5) after the last, so the reading ends with 'the great and awesome day' and not with 'ban'. The same custom is followed at the end of Isaiah, Lamentations and Ecclesiastes. The Greek ends instead with the line on Moses, so its order of the last verses differs (see the variants). Zechariah 14:11 says "no more ban": one more link between the end of the Twelve and the book before it. Russell Fuller, who edited the scroll 4QXIIa in DJD XV, proposed that Jonah follows Malachi in it, so that the Twelve there did not end on Malachi; this is a disputed reconstruction, and the printout used here cannot show the order of the books.
